messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: meta-traits issue
parts:
1. This is only going to affect behavior that's
not yet documented in the manual -- vectorizing matrices,
for instance, m ~ normal(0,1) to give a whole matrix
m a unit normal distirbution.

2. The failing part of the test is here:

and here's the test from:

test/meta/traits_test.cpp, line 227:
-------------------------
const Matrix<double,1,Dynamic> d(c);
VectorView<const Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> > dv(d);
for (size_t n = 0; n < 10; ++n)
EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(d[n], dv[n]);
--------------------------

I'm pretty sure the problem is the way the VectorView
templates are getting instantiated. Here is the
basic class:


template<typename T,
bool is_vec = stan::is_vector<T>::value>
class VectorView

and here are its specializations:

template<typename T>
class VectorView<T*,false>

template<typename T>
class VectorView<T,true>

template<typename T>
class VectorView<T*,true>

template<typename T>
class VectorView<const T,true>

The only one that matches the call in the test should
be the last one, but the behavior looks like the basic
class might be getting instantiated.

Also, I think trying to instantiate VectorView<double*>
would lead to a conflict betwene the first and third
template specialization.


Also, the basic class's definition seems wrong, because
it doesn't actually pay attention to the is_vec
declaration and treats everything as a scalar ptr.

stan/meta/traits.hpp, line 171
-------------------------------
template<typename T,
bool is_vec = stan::is_vector<T>::value>
class VectorView {
private:
T* x_;
public:
VectorView(T& x) : x_(&x) { }
typename scalar_type<T>::type& operator[](int /*i*/) {
return *x_;
}
};
---------------

The is_vec gets a default, but isn't used in the class definition.
Instead, the operator[] definition assumes T is not a vector.

I think the problem might go away if we change the basic class so
that its operator[] definition is:

typename scalar_type<T>::type& operator[](int i) {
if (is_vec) return x_[i];
else return *x_;
}

AND

add Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> to the is_vector type. Or
maybe better, an is_vector<T> || is_matrix<T> so we can
keep the types separate.

The (is_vec) value is known statically, so should get optimized away
in the two instances of the template (is_vec = TRUE, is_vec = FALSE).

Alternatively, I think it could be rewritten. As is, there
are probably unexpected consequences of the definitions such
as the fact that const types are always assumed to be vectors.

Is the behavior we want just this?

scalar-like: double, var

vector-like: double*, var*,
vector<double>, vector<var>,
Matrix<double,R,C>, Matrix<var,R,C>

Reference types T& should behave like the unreferenced type T.
Usually in this kind of setup, so do pointers, but here the
decision was made to treat pointers as arrays.

But we should be able to fix this problem by simply defining
vector views for all these types:

basic, def for scalars:

template <typename T> VectorView

vector-like def:

template <typename T> VectorView<T*>

template <typename T> VectorView<vector<T> >

template <typename T, int R, int C> VectorView<Matrix<T,R,C> >

Of course, we really only need two definitions for vector view,
one for scalars and one for vectors. We could instead have a bunch
of factory functions that return VectorView instances rather than
definining a bunch of VectorView template classes with redundant
definitions.

Daniel -- if this is all too much to digest, we can talk on Monday.

- Bob
